title: General Chemistry II
description: Kinetics, acid-base systems, electrochemistry, and coordination chemistry connected to buffers, redox biology, and metal-dependent biomolecules.

modifications: Expanded the week-5 kinetics and mechanism reading with experimental rate-law comparisons, unit-aware Arrhenius ratios, elementary-step constraints, catalysts, and a limited first-order half-life example; linked both objectives to outcome 2.

Expanded the week-9 redox reading with galvanic-cell components, electrode and cell-potential conventions, unit-aware free-energy calculations, and standard versus nonstandard conditions; clarified both objectives and mapped the lesson to outcome 3.

Expanded the week-12 coordination primer with coordination-sphere and donor counting, formal oxidation-state bookkeeping, geometry limits, a bounded crystal-field model, and protein-environment effects; clarified both objectives and mapped them to outcome 4.

Linked both week-1 weak-acid/buffer objectives to outcome 1. Reassociated the preserved pKa-and-ratio pH calculation with the Henderson–Hasselbalch objective and added direct practice selecting the Ka expression using the weak-acid mass balance; the existing prompts and answer keys are unchanged. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

outcomes.description: Interpret rate laws and activation energy.
Relate redox potential to electron-transfer direction.
Explain coordination geometry and ligand effects.

lesson_objectives.description: Use Ka, pKa, and mass balance to reason about weak acids.
Estimate buffer pH with Henderson-Hasselbalch when assumptions hold.
Infer empirical reaction order from controlled rate data and interpret a first-order half-life.
Relate temperature to rate constants through Arrhenius behavior.
Relate a standard cell potential and electron count to a redox reaction's standard free-energy change.
Calculate a standard cell potential from reduction potentials and infer the direction favored under standard conditions.
Identify a metal center and its donor atoms, and explain how its protein environment can alter redox behavior.
Explain how ligand-field strength changes d-orbital splitting and can affect spin, color, and redox behavior.
Use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to compute the base-to-acid ratio and component concentrations for a buffer at a target pH.
Predict the pH change of a buffer after adding strong acid and compare it with unbuffered water, using buffer capacity to explain the difference.
Calculate the ionized fraction of a weak acid or base at a given pH and evaluate its consequences for membrane permeation.
Use integrated first- and second-order rate laws to compute remaining concentration and half-life.
Determine reaction order from concentration-time data by choosing the transformation that gives a straight line.
Calculate an activation energy from rate constants at two temperatures and predict a rate constant at a third temperature.
Use the Nernst equation to compute the actual reduction potential of a couple from its standard potential and the ratio of oxidized to reduced forms.
Predict the direction of electron transfer between two couples and compute the free-energy change from their potential difference.
Explain coordination number, geometry and ligand effects for biological metal centers, and calculate the free metal ion left after chelation.
Calculate free energy and temperature comparisons with consistent units.
Relate standard/current free energy to equilibrium and composition.
Distinguish reaction coupling, work bounds and kinetic information.
Calculate diprotic acid fractions under declared ideal conventions.
Reconcile family mass balance, spectator charge and water contributions.
Evaluate imposed-pH and approximation domains.
Infer empirical orders, constants and species-rate conventions.
Derive and qualify a pre-equilibrium mechanism rate law.
Evaluate pseudo-first-order and mechanism-identification limits.
Calculate conserved reversible trajectories and equilibrium plateaus.
Resolve relaxation, directional constants and half-life definitions.
Compare sequential intermediate kinetics and observation limitations.
Calculate cell potentials using matching activity/reduction conventions.
Relate electrochemical potential, reaction free energy and equation scaling.
Account for charge and stipulated target current efficiency.
Distinguish donor counts, charge and geometry evidence.
Solve ligand and metal balances under distinct boundary conditions.
Compare limited octahedral occupations and pairing energies.
Calculate saturation and solubility with correct stoichiometry.
Combine ideal complexation, ligand and solubility constraints.
Qualify saturation and separation interpretations.
Summarize concentration reports and correct a supplied reference background.
Fit a reversible relaxation using independent equilibrium composition and a reserved prediction.
Distinguish reporting correction, plateau models and causal-identification limits.
Use the equivalence volume to find an unknown concentration, and identify the stoichiometric regions of a titration curve.

Calculate pH at the start, in the buffer region, at equivalence and beyond equivalence for strong-acid and weak-acid titrations with a strong base, and check the shortcuts against an exact charge balance.

Explain why the equivalence pH of a weak-acid titration lies above 7, read pKa from the half-equivalence point, choose an indicator whose transition brackets the equivalence pH, and locate the equivalence points of a diprotic acid.
Use protonation and finite ligand totals in a coupled binding equation.
Reconstruct each free/protonated pool and verify amount conservation.
Check an imposed pH against the spectator inventory required by charge balance.
Reject inadmissible states and verify the original equations.
Keep formal electron count, occupation and spin bookkeeping separate.
Convert an assigned photon energy and compare stipulated field/pairing energies.
Combine occupation energy with a qualified spin-only moment.
Extend field occupation bookkeeping beyond one electron count.
Evaluate a saturating reduced rate with its parameter combinations.
Recognize two mechanisms sharing the same reduced observation curve.
Use a discriminating reduced-model prediction rather than only more shared-curve points.
Quantify the steady-intermediate and time-scale assumptions.
Solve and reconstruct a distinct closed ligand/proton/charge state.
Close the water, pH, bound-fraction and spectator ledgers.
Recover a different reduced hyperbola without identifying it as a unique mechanism.
Predict an informative comparison and retain its model limits.
Apply assigned spectral energy without treating a simplified spin calculation as full structure evidence.
Derive a conditional potential from free-versus-total redox species.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 11-week local sequence groups each compact buffer, kinetics, redox and coordination primer with its expanded treatment; all 15 topic lessons and the synthetic lab remain scheduled, and weeks 8–9 add an optional redox-cell project guide with rehearsal practice and milestone self-checks. Workload and qualified review are absent; no semester equivalence is established.

workload.basis: Not measured. Legacy nominal credit and display-time labels are not retained as workload estimates.

lessons.title: Acid-base equilibria and buffers
lessons.worked_example: At pH=pKa the buffer ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is approximately one. Adding 1 mmol of strong acid to a synthetic buffer with 10 mmol of each form first changes the amounts to 9 mmol A⁻ and 11 mmol HA; recalculate pH from the new ratio, not the starting amounts.

lessons.title: Kinetics and reaction mechanisms
lessons.worked_example: A first-order reaction with k = 0.35 min⁻¹ has t½ = ln 2/k = 1.98 min; the inverse-time units cancel. For a separate Arrhenius comparison with Ea = 50.0 kJ/mol, convert to 50,000 J/mol before using R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). From 298 K to 308 K, ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/298 − 1/308) = 0.655, giving a rate-constant factor of e⁰·⁶⁵⁵ = 1.93. This is a model-based ratio, not an absolute reaction rate.

lessons.title: Redox and electrochemical cells
lessons.worked_example: For the Zn/Cu cell, E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. With n = 2, ΔG° = −nFE°cell = −212 kJ/mol. For a separate cell with n = 2 and E°cell = +0.30 V, ΔG° = −57.9 kJ/mol. Keep reduction potentials as tabulated, subtract the anode value, and convert joules to kilojoules. The potential remains unchanged if the balanced equation is scaled.

modules.title: Coordination chemistry and biologically relevant metals

lessons.title: Coordination chemistry and biologically relevant metals
lessons.worked_example: For [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂, the bracketed ion has charge +2; neutral NH₃ and one inner-sphere Cl⁻ give cobalt oxidation state +3. Five ammonia donors plus one chloride donor give coordination number six. In a separate octahedral model, strong-field ligands increase Δₒ and may favor low spin for suitable d counts, but do not by themselves specify a redox-potential shift.

lessons.title: Buffers by design: Henderson–Hasselbalch, capacity and the ionization of weak acids and bases
lessons.worked_example: For pKa 6.86 and pH 7.4, [A⁻]/[HA] = 3.467, giving 77.6 mM base and 22.4 mM acid in 100 mM buffer; adding 10 mmol acid per liter lowers pH only to 7.18; capacity is 40.0 mM per pH unit.

lessons.title: Rate laws in practice: integrated forms, half-lives, Arrhenius temperature dependence and how to tell the order
lessons.worked_example: With k = 0.0231 min⁻¹, t½ = 30.0 min and 25.0% remains after 60 min; rate constants 1.0×10⁻³ and 2.6×10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 298.15 and 310.15 K give Ea = 61.2 kJ/mol, predicting 1.54×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at 277.15 K.

lessons.title: Redox direction and metal centers: the Nernst equation, electron flow and why ligands matter
lessons.worked_example: At [NAD⁺]/[NADH] = 10, E = -0.2892 V; transfer to a 0.045 V acceptor has ΔE = 0.3342 V and ΔG = -64.5 kJ/mol; with K_f = 10⁷ M⁻¹, 1 mM complex and 1 mM free EDTA leave 0.1 μM free Ca²⁺.

modules.title: Free energy, equilibrium and reaction direction

lessons.title: Free energy, equilibrium and reaction direction
lessons.worked_example: Convert 50.0 J/(mol·K) to 0.0500 kJ/(mol·K), then calculate 12.0−300×0.0500=−3.0 kJ/mol. Convert back to joules for K=exp(3000/(8.314×300)). For Q=10, add RT ln 10 to the standard free energy and obtain positive current ΔG. For the separate ideal A/B inventory with total 1.0 mol/L, combine K with conservation instead of claiming complete conversion. Finally, combine compatible constants 4 and 0.5 to obtain net K=2.

modules.title: Coupled acid speciation and charge balance

lessons.title: Coupled acid speciation and charge balance
lessons.worked_example: At h=10⁻⁶, divide the denominator terms by h² to obtain 1,10,0.1. Normalize by 11.1 and multiply each fraction by C_T=0.0100. Compute family negative charge with one weight for HA⁻ and two for A²⁻. Add hydroxide 10⁻⁸ mol/L and subtract h to find the required spectator difference. This calculation gives both a normalized species table and the spectator inventory compatible with the imposed pH.

lessons.title: Rate laws and mechanism inference
lessons.worked_example: Take initial-rate ratios 4 for a twofold A increase and 2 for a twofold B increase. Solve 2^m=4 and 2^n=2, giving m=2,n=1. Compute k from the reference mixture and predict the new rate 0.00675. For the separate hypothetical pre-equilibrium mechanism, calculate I from K_c[A][B], then form k₂[I]. Keep the empirical example and proposed mechanism separate: they describe different synthetic models and do not claim to explain the same reaction.

lessons.title: Reversible and sequential kinetics
lessons.worked_example: Add the reversible constants to obtain λ=0.060 and use the reverse fraction of that sum to find A_eq=0.20. Calculate A at 20 min and recover B from conserved total. Distinguish displacement half-life from time to A=0.50. In the separate chain, differentiate the intermediate expression or set its production equal to removal, find the peak time and check the conserved amounts 0.25+0.50+0.25=1. These calculations describe two different kinetic structures.

lessons.title: Electrochemical stoichiometry, composition and work
lessons.worked_example: Subtract the stipulated reduction values for E°=0.50 V. Form −2×96485×0.50 and convert joules to kilojoules for ΔG°. At Q=100, subtract the natural-log composition term for E≈0.440478. Double the whole equation and verify that potential stays fixed while reaction free energy doubles. Separately, use 0.50×120=60 C, divide by 2F and apply the stated 80% current efficiency to calculate target amount.

lessons.title: Ligand balance and coordination models
lessons.worked_example: Set complex concentration x and subtract it from both analytical totals. Solve x=10⁴(0.0010−x)(0.0015−x), retain the bounded root and reconstruct both free species. Check K_f and both totals. Separately count six donors from three bidentate ligands. For the distinct d⁶ model, compare lower/upper occupations and add the pairing-cost difference to obtain −100 kJ/mol. These examples do not identify one real complex.

lessons.title: Solubility, complexation and competing equilibria
lessons.worked_example: For MX in pure water, use s²=10⁻⁸. For common-ion conditions, retain s in 0.0100+s and check the small-change approximation. For MX₂, use 4s³ rather than s². In the fixed-free-ligand example, form 1+K_fl=101, solve for total S, then divide by 101 for free metal. Check the metal and charge totals before interpreting the larger dissolved amount.

modules.title: Acid–base titration curves: equivalence, buffer regions and indicators

lessons.title: Acid–base titration curves: equivalence, buffer regions and indicators
lessons.worked_example: Titrating 25.00 mL of 0.100 M weak acid (pK_a 4.76) with 0.100 M NaOH gives pH 2.88 at the start, 4.76 at 12.50 mL, 5.36 at 20.00 mL, 8.73 at the 25.00 mL equivalence point and 11.29 at 26.00 mL; an exact charge balance agrees within 0.001 pH. An indicator changing near 8.2–10.0 brackets the equivalence pH; one changing near 3.8–5.4 would change in the buffer region.

modules.title: Virtual lab 1: reporting background and reversible relaxation

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: reporting background and reversible relaxation
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic blank identifies 0.0500 mM reporting background. Independent equilibrium A=0.20 mM defines a separate physical plateau. The t00/t20 displacement fit gives λ≈0.059991 min⁻¹ and a reserved t60 prediction; this checks the construction without identifying a real mechanism.

lessons.title: Redox project guide: a fictional cell from electron balance to charge accounting (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For fictional tokens X and Y with X³⁺ + 3e⁻ ⇌ X(s), E° = −0.100 V, and Y⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Y(s), E° = +0.350 V, the balanced cell X(s) + 3Y⁺ → X³⁺ + 3Y(s) has n = 3 and E°cell = 0.450 V, so ΔG° ≈ −130.3 kJ/mol and ln K ≈ 52.55. Passing 144 C at 100% Faradaic efficiency consumes about 0.0004975 mol X.

modules.title: Proton-coupled complexation with finite ligand pools

lessons.title: Proton-coupled complexation with finite ligand pools
lessons.worked_example: Alpha=Ka/(Ka+h)=1/3 and Kf alpha=1250 L/mol. The admissible root of x=1250(0.0015−x)(0.0021−x) is 0.0009 mol/L. This conditional equation uses the unbound ligand pool, not analytical LT as a free-species concentration. Reconstruct the free species and verify both original amount balances before accepting this conditional result.

modules.title: Ligand-field occupations, spin and spectral evidence

lessons.title: Ligand-field occupations, spin and spectral evidence
lessons.worked_example: Formal count is d5. High spin has lower/upper occupation 3/2 with five unpaired electrons and no pairs. Low spin has five lower electrons, two pairs and one unpaired electron. Formal oxidation is bookkeeping, not a direct measured metal charge.

lessons.title: Ligand-exchange kinetics and mechanism discrimination
lessons.worked_example: The capture coefficient kc[Y] is 0.06 s−1, matching the return coefficient. Thus the reduced kobs is 0.0002 s−1, half of plateau kd=0.0004. Half-plateau occurs at Y=kr[L]/kc=0.0006 mol/L. These refer to the declared reduction, not an exact universal microscopic law.

lessons.title: Assignment 1: closed-solution equilibrium ledger
lessons.worked_example: The coupled positive-h state has h=10^−6 mol/L and alpha=0.8. Complex is 0.0008, free metal 0.0004 and free L− 0.0008 mol/L, leaving HL=0.0002. Both totals, the original formation/acid relations and the fixed spectator charge must agree; one matching concentration alone is insufficient.

modules.title: Assignment 2: mechanism evidence and reduction report

lessons.title: Assignment 2: mechanism evidence and reduction report
lessons.worked_example: At Y=0.0005, kcY=0.04 matches the return coefficient, so the rate is half of 0.0006: 0.0003 s−1. The corresponding rapid-association model with KA=2000 L/mol and kturn=0.0006 has the same reduced curve. Fit quality alone cannot resolve that structural ambiguity.

modules.title: Assignment 3: coordination evidence and conditional redox ledger

lessons.title: Assignment 3: coordination evidence and conditional redox ledger
lessons.worked_example: The assigned photon energy is about 184.04087 kJ/mol. Low-minus-high energy is +5.95913 kJ/mol, favoring the high-spin d4 candidate with four unpaired electrons and moment sqrt(24) under the spin-only assumptions. This does not supply a real spin population, geometry or complete free energy.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added two original lessons (buffer design, capacity and ionization of weak acids and bases; integrated rate laws, reaction order from data and Arrhenius temperature dependence) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on the Nernst equation, electron-transfer direction, biological metal coordination and chelation with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added seven original lessons on free energy, coupled acid speciation, empirical/mechanistic rate laws, reversible/sequential kinetics, electrochemical accounting, ligand balance and solubility/complexation; one synthetic reference-and-plateau relaxation lab and a proposed weekly schedule. Developed with Codex assistance. Still partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-1 acid/base reading with Ka and mass-balance reasoning, a qualified Henderson–Hasselbalch derivation, stoichiometric neutralization before re-equilibration, and total-concentration/buffer-capacity distinctions. Existing questions, keys and objectives are unchanged. Three compact prototype readings remain in weeks 5, 9 and 12; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-5 kinetics reading with controlled initial-rate comparisons, empirical rate-law units, Arrhenius temperature ratios, mechanism constraints, catalysis and a limited first-order half-life check. Clarified the first objective to cover the preserved half-life item and linked both objectives and the assessment to outcome 2. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged. Two compact prototype readings remain in weeks 9 and 12; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-9 redox and electrochemical-cells reading with oxidation/reduction conventions, galvanic-cell components, standard reduction potentials, electron-flow and voltage signs, ΔG° from nFE°, and the limits of standard-state predictions. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the practice assessment to outcome 3. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged. One compact prototype reading remains in week 12; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded the week-12 coordination reading with coordination spheres, donor-atom counting, formal oxidation-state bookkeeping, geometry limits, ligand-field splitting, spin/color qualifications and protein-environment effects. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the practice assessment to outcome 4. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged. All four original compact prototype readings now have expanded instruction; the package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Linked both week-1 weak-acid/buffer objectives to outcome 1. Reassociated the preserved pKa-and-ratio check with the Henderson–Hasselbalch objective and added direct practice using the weak-acid mass balance to form Ka; existing prompts and keys are unchanged. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an inactive fictional-redox portfolio combining balanced half-reactions, standard cell potential, Gibbs energy, equilibrium, a Nernst correction and Faraday amount accounting. The abstract species and values are not a real chemical cell; the package remains partial and formative-only.

Regrouped compact buffer, kinetics, redox and coordination readings with their expanded treatments, preserving every lesson, assessment and question ID. The resulting proposed sequence has 11 active weeks including the existing lab, not 14 calendar blocks for repeated introductions. Clarified that Chemistry I/II are local segments of one MIT 5.111SC comparator. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Grouped an original acid–base titration-curve reading with the week-3 coupled-speciation lesson: equivalence and endpoint, the four regions of weak- and strong-acid curves checked against an exact charge balance, indicator choice and diprotic equivalence volumes. Added three objectives, eleven formative items and four cards, with no week added. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Made the planned fictional redox-cell project usable by learners as ungraded practice. Week 8 gains an optional project guide with the project's half-reactions, inputs and tasks, a worked example on a separate fictional cell, a rehearsal cell and five open rehearsal practice items; five project milestones are Case studio self-checks with a week-9 project record. The relaxation lab's dataset link now points to the package-pinned CSV instead of a mutable repository URL; a week-10 solubility expression, S=[M]·(1+K_fl), no longer renders as a link; and two stale counts in the limitations and structure note (a 14-week scope and 14 lessons) now match the 11-week, 15-lesson sequence. The inactive project draft is unchanged; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added original finite-pool proton/ligand/charge, extended field/spin/spectral and competing ligand-exchange mechanism foundations; three connected equilibrium/evidence/redox reports; eighteen checkpoint items/cards and an analytic reduced-rate CSV. Explicitly distinguishes closed/reservoir boundaries, reduced observations from unique mechanisms and free/total redox species. Preserves the existing relaxation lab and fictional redox project. All systems are synthetic, partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: All four compact prototype readings now share topic weeks with their expanded treatments in the proposed 11-week sequence; the course remains partial and is not a full university semester.

The proposed 11-week scope is unmeasured and unreviewed; no graded homework sequence, exams or full laboratory sequence exists. An optional redox-cell project guide with rehearsal practice and Case studio milestone self-checks (weeks 8–9) is ungraded practice; the separate cumulative-project draft stays inactive.
Public practice points are study feedback, not course grades. All keys/feedback remain public formative authoring specifications.
All new parameters and observations are synthetic, with explicitly restricted ideal, concentration-form or kinetic assumptions; no handling protocol or biological recommendation is supplied.
Subject-matter, accessibility and workload review remain outstanding; objective associations are provisional.
Eleven primary OpenStax Chemistry 2e section pages are registered as link-only references; no prose, problem, figure or dataset was imported.

General Chemistry I/II is a local division of topics compared against one integrated MIT 5.111SC course. General Chemistry I introduces buffer and calibration ideas; this package develops coupled speciation and continues kinetics, redox, coordination and complexation. The pair does not claim two MIT-equivalent courses.

The fictional redox-cell project is optional and ungraded. Its five milestones are Case studio self-checks whose private drafts are never submitted or scored; the rehearsal practice uses a separate fictional cell, and no software check evaluates a learner's project calculations or written interpretation. Milestone weeks are planning suggestions, not measured workload or deadlines.

Three new selected foundations and three open reports deepen closed proton/ligand/charge balances, field/spin/spectral bookkeeping, competing reduced exchange models and free-to-total redox factors. Reduced-rate CSV values are analytic, not measured or exact full-network trajectories. Browser checkpoints do not evaluate written chemical reasoning, solvers, proposed studies or real molecular evidence. Additional speciation/activity/coordination kinetics and broader coursework/lab depth remain incomplete; workload and qualified review are open. The 11 grouped blocks retain the local split of one primary comparator.

Of the 131 numerical answers, 10 require units, 49 check significant figures and 0 check dimensions. New continuous checkpoint quantities request three significant figures, except logarithmic pH requests three decimal places with a numeric tolerance rather than a significant-figure rule; exact electron/pair counts have no significant-figure requirement. Output formatting is not a claim about measurement uncertainty.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, complete laboratory sequence, activated cumulative project, measured workload and qualified human review remain outstanding.
